text: Johnson will not rest the case upon his own admiration, which might be no more than the admiration of one age and of one temper. He inquires instead what time has done to the work. A writer whose fame is built upon the fashion of his day, upon local customs, or upon the quarrels of a party, may be praised so long as that fashion lasts; the fashion passes, however, and the praise goes with it. Those works alone can be said to have proved their worth which continue to please readers who share none of the circumstances of their first audience; for such readers come to the trial without partiality. They have no friendship with the author, and no stake in his opinions; they read him for no other reason than that he still gives them pleasure.
